On the uniqueness of even LpL_{p}-Minkowski problem

Weiyong He Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR 97403. Email address: whe@uoregon.edu and Junbang Liu Address: Department of Mathematics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Clear Water Bay. Email address: junbangliu@ust.hk
Abstract.

We prove that there is a unique p0∈[0,1)p_{0}\in[0,1), which can be characterized by the eigenvalue of Hilbert operator related to a convex body, that the even LpL^{p} Minkowski problem has a unique solution for p≥p0p\geq p_{0}, and the uniqueness fails for infinitely many convex bodies if p<p0p<p_{0}. The previous results by many experts in the field assert that the uniqueness holds for p>p0p>p_{0}.

1. Introduction

The Minkowski problem forms the core of various areas in fully nonlinear partial differential equations and convex geometry (see Trudinger, Wang [48] and Schneider [45]), which was extended to the LpL_{p}-Minkowski theory by Lutwak [33, 34, 35] where p=1p=1 corresponds to the classical case. The classical Minkowski’s existence theorem due to Minkowski and Aleksandrov characterizes the surface area measure SKS_{K} of a convex body KK in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, more precisely, it solves the Monge-Ampŕe equation

det(∇2h+h​Id)=f\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\;\text{Id})=f

on the sphere SnS^{n} where a convex body KK with C+2C^{2}_{+} boundary provides a solution if h=hK|Snh=h_{K}|_{S^{n}} for the support function hKh_{K} of KK, and in this case, 1/f⁡(x)1/f(x) is the Gaussian curvature at the y∈∂Ky\in\partial K where xx is an exterior normal of x∈Snx\in S^{n}. One may consult Cheng-Yau [21] and Pogorelov [40] for a full discussion on the Minkowski problem and its resolution. The so-called log-Minkowski problem

h​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f (1)

or L0L_{0}-Minkowski problem was posed by Firey [23] in his seminal paper, which seeks to characterize the cone volume measure

d​VK=1n+1​hK​d​SKdV_{K}=\frac{1}{n+1}h_{K}dS_{K}

of a convex body KK containing the origin o∈ℝn+1o\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, and to determine whether the even solution is unique if ff is even. The latter problem is the so-called Log-Minkowski conjecture by Lutwak. The log-Minkowski problem has received due attention only after Lutwak’s LpL_{p} Minkowski problem

h1−p​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh^{1-p}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f (2)

in the 1990’s where p=1p=1 and p=0p=0 are the classical and the logarithmic Minkowski problem.

The uniqueness of the solution of the classical Minkowski problem up to translation is the consequence of the equality case of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality

V​(α​L+β​K)1n+1≥α​V​(L)1n+1+β​V​(K)1n+1V(\alpha L+\beta K)^{\frac{1}{n+1}}\geq\alpha V(L)^{\frac{1}{n+1}}+\beta V(K)^{\frac{1}{n+1}} (3)

for convex bodies LL and KK, α,β≥0\alpha,\beta\geq 0. For p≥0p\geq 0, the LpL_{p} Minkowski problem is intimately related to the LpL_{p} version of the conjectured Brunn-Minkowski inequality

V((1−λ)L+pλK)≥((1−λ)V(L)pn+1+λV(K)pn+1)n+1pV((1-\lambda)L+_{p}\lambda K)\geq\left((1-\lambda)V(L)^{\frac{p}{n+1}}+\lambda V(K)^{\frac{p}{n+1}}\right)^{\frac{n+1}{p}} (4)

for λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) and convex bodies L,KL,K containing the origin. The case p=0p=0 is interpreted as the limit case

V((1−λ)L+0λK)≥V(L)1−λV(K)λ.V((1-\lambda)L+_{0}\lambda K)\geq V(L)^{1-\lambda}V(K)^{\lambda}.

When p=1p=1, (4) is the classical Brunn-Minkowski inequality and a theorem of Firey [22], for p>1p>1, where he introduced the LpL_{p} Minkowski sum of convex bodies for p>1p>1. The notion was then extended by Böröczky, Lutwak, Yang and Zhang [7] for p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1). Assuming L,KL,K are origin symmetric, the even LpL_{p} Brunn-Minkowski conjecture states that (4) holds for p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1) [7, Problem 1.1, 1.5], in which the conjecture was established for n=1n=1. The conjecture is known to be equivalent to the even LpL_{p}-Minkowski inequality (conjecture) [7, Lemma 3.1].

Conjecture 1 (Böröczky-Lutwak-Yang-Zhang, Even LpL_{p} Brunn-Minkowski conjecture).

For any origin-symmetric convex bodies in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, (4) holds for p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1). Moreover, it is equivalent to

1p​∫SnhLp​hK1−p​d​SK≥n+1p​V​(K)1−pn+1​V​(L)pn+1.\frac{1}{p}\int_{S^{n}}h_{L}^{p}h_{K}^{1-p}dS_{K}\geq\frac{n+1}{p}V(K)^{1-\frac{p}{n+1}}V(L)^{\frac{p}{n+1}}. (5)

The case p=0p=0 is interpreted as the limit case, known as the conjectured Log-Minkowski inequality,

1V⁡(K)​∫Snlog⁡hLhK​d​VK≥1n+1​log⁡V⁡(L)V⁡(K).\frac{1}{V(K)}\int_{S^{n}}\log\frac{h_{L}}{h_{K}}dV_{K}\geq\frac{1}{n+1}\log\frac{V(L)}{V(K)}. (6)

This family of inequalities has attracted much interest, see for instance [20, 24, 32, 37, 42, 43, 44, 53, 29, 16, 41, 9, 39, 52] etc. The conjectured inequalities above for even convex bodies are essentially equivalent to the following LpL_{p}-Minkowski conjecture,

Conjecture 2.

For p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), the Monge-Ampere equation on SnS^{n}

h1−p​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh^{1-p}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f

has a unique even solution if ff is a positive even smooth function on SnS^{n}.

There are some substantial progress for the conjectures. When f=1f=1, the uniqueness problem receives special attention since the work of Firey [23] and its relation with the Gauss curvature flow [17, 1, 3]. The uniqueness is proved for p∈(−n−1,1)p\in(-n-1,1) without assuming the even condition by Brendle, Choi and Daskalopoulos [11] when ff is a constant. For general even function ff, there are also considerate important progress towards the uniqueness conjecture, notably by Kolesnikov and Milman [29] and Chen, Huang, Li, Liu [16]. We introduce necessary notations. Let KK be a compact convex set in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. The support function of KK is defined as hK:ℝn+1→ℝ,hK​(x)=maxy∈K⁡x⋅yh_{K}:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R},h_{K}(x)=\max_{y\in K}x\cdot y. Let u∈Snu\in S^{n}, then we call uu is an outer unit normal of KK at a boundary point yy if y⋅u=hK​(u)y\cdot u=h_{K}(u). A boundary point is said to be singular if it has more than one unit normal vector, and it’s well-known that the set of singular points has Hausdorff measure ℋn{\mathcal{H}}^{n} equal to 0. Let νK:∂K→Sn\nu_{K}:\partial K\rightarrow S^{n} be the generalized Gauss map. For each Borel set ω∈Sn\omega\in S^{n}, define SK​(ω):=ℋn​(νK−1​(ω))S_{K}(\omega):={\mathcal{H}}^{n}(\nu_{K}^{-1}(\omega)). The measure SKS_{K} on SnS^{n} is called the Aleksandrov-Fenchel-Jessen surface area measure of KK. For any two convex bodies K,L∈ℝn+1K,L\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), p∈(0,∞)p\in(0,\infty), one defines the LpL_{p}-Minkowski sum (1−λ)L+pλK(1-\lambda)L+_{p}\lambda K as

(1−λ)L+pλK:=∩x∈Sn{y∈ℝn+1:y⋅x≤(1−λ)hLp(x)+λhKp(x)}.(1-\lambda)L+_{p}\lambda K:=\cap_{x\in S^{n}}\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:y\cdot x\leq(1-\lambda)h_{L}^{p}(x)+\lambda h_{K}^{p}(x)\}. (7)

The limit case p=0p=0 is interpreted as

(1−λ)L+0λK:=∩x∈Sn{y∈ℝn+1:y⋅x≤hL1−λ(x)hKλ(x)}.(1-\lambda)L+_{0}\lambda K:=\cap_{x\in S^{n}}\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:y\cdot x\leq h_{L}^{1-\lambda}(x)h_{K}^{\lambda}(x)\}. (8)

In the following, we use 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} to denote the set of all convex bodies in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, and let 𝒦e{\mathcal{K}}_{e} be the set of origin-symmetric bodies in 𝒦{\mathcal{K}}. 𝒦+,e2{\mathcal{K}}_{+,e}^{2} is the set of convex bodies with C2C^{2}-boundary and strictly positive curvature, in other words, the support function of convex body KK in 𝒦+,e2{\mathcal{K}}_{+,e}^{2} is a C2C^{2} even function with ∇2hK+hK​Id>0\nabla^{2}h_{K}+h_{K}\text{Id}>0.

LK​z=h−1​HKi​j​(hk2​zi)j,L_{K}z=h^{-1}H_{K}^{ij}(h_{k}^{2}z_{i})_{j}, (9)

Kolesnikov and Milman [29] formulated the following local LpL^{p}-Minkowski conjecture for a symmetric convex body K∈𝒦+,e2K\in{\mathcal{K}}_{+,e}^{2} (we use slighly different notations).

Conjecture 3 (Local LpL_{p}-Minkowski conjecture, Kolesnikov-Milman).

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1). For all K∈𝒦+,e2K\in{\mathcal{K}}_{+,e}^{2}, and z∈Ce2​(Sn)z\in C^{2}_{e}(S^{n}) with ∫Snz​hK​d​SK=0\int_{S^{n}}zh_{K}dS_{K}=0, one has

Conjecture 4 (Local log-Minkowski conjecture, Kolesnikov-Milman).

When restricted on the subspace EevenE_{\text{even}} of even functions, the eigenvalue of −LK-L_{K} satisfies

λ1,e​(−LK)≥n+1.\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K})\geq n+1.

There exists pn∈(0,1)p_{n}\in(0,1) of the form pn=1−cn−3/2p_{n}=1-cn^{-3/2} such that, for all K∈𝒦+,e2K\in{\mathcal{K}}_{+,e}^{2},

By recent progress on the KLS conjecture [19] and results in [29], one can get that pnp_{n} is of the form 1−cϵ​n−1−ϵ1-c_{\epsilon}n^{-1-\epsilon} see [39, 6] for more details. Relying on the local uniqueness theorem above, Chen, Huang, Li, Liu [16] proved LpL_{p} Minkowski conjecture for p∈(pn,1)p\in(p_{n},1) using the continuity method in elliptic PDE theory, and they also proved the uniqueness when ff is sufficiently closed to 11 (or a constant) and even.

Theorem 2 (Chen-Huang-Li-Liu).

Let p∈(pn,1)p\in(p_{n},1). the Monge-Ampere equation on SnS^{n}

h1−p​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh^{1-p}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f

has a unique even solution if ff is a positive even smooth function on SnS^{n}.

When ff is closed to a constant but not assumed to be even, there are some recent progress as well [15, 10]. In this paper we continue to investigate the uniqueness of the even LpL_{p} Minkowski problem, after the progress in [29, 16, 41]. Let p0∈[0,1)p_{0}\in[0,1) such that

infK∈𝒦+,e2λ1,e​(−LK)=n+1−p0.\inf_{K\in{\mathcal{K}}^{2}_{+,e}}\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K})=n+1-p_{0}. (11)

Our main theorem can be stated as follows,

Theorem 3.

The even LpL_{p} Minkowski conjecture holds for p=p0p=p_{0}; that is,

h1−p0​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh^{1-p_{0}}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f

has a unique smooth even solution if ff is a positive even smooth function on SnS^{n}. Moreover, for any K∈𝒦+,e4K\in{\mathcal{K}}^{4}_{+,e}, we have

λ1,e​(−LK)>n+1−p0.\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K})>n+1-p_{0}. (12)

For each p∈(−n−1,p0)p\in(-n-1,p_{0}), there exists infinitely many positive smooth even functions ff, the equation

h1−p​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh^{1-p}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f

has at least two even smooth solutions.

The non-uniqueness result in Theorem 3 was derived by E. Milman in [38, Corollary 1.5] as a direct consequence of the fact that infλ1,e≤n+1\inf\lambda_{1,e}\leq n+1. We include the statement in our theorem for completeness. Chen, Huang, Li, Liu [16] proved that the even LpL_{p} Minkowski conjecture holds for (p0,1)(p_{0},1). Our improvement is to prove that the uniqueness conjecture actually holds at p0p_{0} as well. In short we can say that the uniqueness is closed if it is open in pp. Our result is a consequence of the following,

Theorem 4.

Suppose for p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), the LpL_{p}-Brunn-Minkowski inequality (5) holds, then

h1−p​det(∇2h+h​Id)=fh^{1-p}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})=f

has a unique smooth even solution if ff is a positive even smooth function on SnS^{n}.

The equivalence between the even LpL_{p} Brunn-Minkowski conjectures and the even LpL_{p} Minkowski conjecture are well-known, see [7] and in particular [39, Theorem 1.1, Theorem 2.1] for the most recent update. In particular Putterman [41, Proposition 1.5] proved that a local version of LpL_{p}-Brunn-Minkowski inequality implies the global version of the inequality, verifying a conjecture in [29]. Her results in particular imply that the LpL_{p}-Brunn-Minkowski inequalities hold at p=p0p=p_{0}. Our result above (Theorem 4) provides one missing piece in the picture of the equivalence of these conjectures. The other new ingredient of our result is to provide the strict eigenvalue estimate (12). We actually prove the following,

Theorem 5.

For K∈𝒦+,e4K\in{\mathcal{K}}^{4}_{+,e}, then λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) cannot have a local minimum.

As this manuscript was being completed, we note that S. Wang also obtained similar results in[50], where he proved that if the local log Brunn-Minkowski inequality holds, then the equality occurs only for homothetic convex bodies. It’s equivalent to that λ1,e​(−LK)>0\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K})>0. However, our approach here is very different from [50]. Kolesnikov and Milamn [29, Proposition 5.14] conjectured that infλ1,e\inf\lambda_{1,e} is taken by the cube, which is known to be n+1n+1 [29, Theorem 10.2] (note that we use a different normalization and dimension convention). Our result shows that if the conjecture infλ1,e=n+1\inf\lambda_{1,e}=n+1 is true, then indeed λ1,e​(−LK)>n+1\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K})>n+1 for any K∈𝒦+,e4K\in{\mathcal{K}}^{4}_{+,e}. For p<0p<0, it is known that both (4) and (5) fail in general and there are many previous known non-uniqueness results [47, 2, 18, 28, 26, 30, 31, 29] etc. The LpL_{p} Brunn-Minkowski theory and LpL_{p} Minkowski problem have attract much attention over last several decades after the seminal work of Lutwak [35], see for instance [4, 5, 8, 14, 18, 25, 27, 36, 46, 49, 54, 55] etc. The existence and uniqueness of the LpL_{p} Minkowski problem are well understood when p≥1p\geq 1. When p<0p<0, the uniqueness fails even restricted to smooth origin-symmetric convex bodies [28]. When 0≤p<10\leq p<1, the uniqueness of solutions to the LpL_{p}-Minkowski problem turns out to be really challenging and it remains a very important open problem in the field. We refer in particular to the recent survey paper by K. Böröczky [6] and [29, 39] for an overview and more references of the problem and related topics in the subject.

The work of Kolesnikov and Milman [29] indicates the significance of the study of the first even eigenvalue λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) for the uniqueness conjecture of the even Logarithm Minkowski problem. Built on the progress in [29, 16, 41], our results above give a characterization of the uniqueness to the even LpL_{p} Minkowski conjecture. In [38], E. Milman provides an elegant proof that the maximum of λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) equals 2​(n+1)2(n+1), and the maximum is achieved precisely by all the ellipsoids. The study of infimum turns out to be much more delicate. For nonsmooth convex body KK, −LK-L_{K} does not have an apparent meaning as a regular differential operator. There are several notions of λ1,e\lambda_{1,e} introduced for nonsmooth case [29, 41, 38], see in particular [38, Section 1.4] for a detailed discussion. It is proved [29] that λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) is invariant under the action of a general linear transformation of ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1},

λ1,e​(−LT⁡(K))=λ1,e​(−LK),T∈G​L​(n+1).\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{T(K)})=\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}),T\in GL(n+1).

Here we give an alternative definition of the first even eigenvalue when a convex body is not smooth. We introduce a complex notation. We embed ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} into ℝn+1×𝕋n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{T}^{n+1}, where 𝕋n+1\mathbb{T}^{n+1} is a standard torus. Using the coordinate x∈ℝn+1x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1} and y∈𝕋n+1y\in\mathbb{T}^{n+1}, we have a standard complex structure on ℝn+1×𝕋n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{T}^{n+1} with the coordinate z=x+−1​yz=x+\sqrt{-1}y. The support function hh, as a homogeneous convex function on ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, can be viewed as to a plurisubharmonic function on ℝn+1×𝕋n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{T}^{n+1}, simply extending hh to be constant along each 𝕋n+1\mathbb{T}^{n+1} fiber. For a given function uu on SnS^{n}, it can also be extended as a homogenous function in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} and hence a function on ℝn+1×𝕋n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{T}^{n+1}. Then we have the following,

Hi​j​ui​uj​h2​det(H)​(−1)n+1​d​Z∧d​Z¯=cn​−1​∂u∧∂¯​u∧Bn,H^{ij}u_{i}u_{j}h^{2}\det(H)(\sqrt{-1})^{n+1}dZ\wedge d\bar{Z}=c_{n}\sqrt{-1}\partial u\wedge\bar{\partial}u\wedge B^{n},

where BB is the (1,1)(1,1) form on ℝn+1×𝕋n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{T}^{n+1},

B=−1​∂∂¯​h+−1​∂r∧∂¯​r,B=\sqrt{-1}\partial\bar{\partial}h+\sqrt{-1}\partial r\wedge\bar{\partial}r,

and r=|x|r=|x| is the radial function on ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, extended to ℝn+1×𝕋n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times\mathbb{T}^{n+1} trivially in the 𝕋n+1\mathbb{T}^{n+1} fiber. As a direct consequence of well known facts in complex pluripotential theory,

−1​∂u∧∂¯​u∧Bn\sqrt{-1}\partial u\wedge\bar{\partial}u\wedge B^{n}

depends continuously on hh (in the L∞L^{\infty} topology). As a direct application, for any u∈Ce2​(Sn)u\in C^{2}_{e}(S^{n}), we have a well defined Radon measure for a convex body in 𝒦e{\mathcal{K}}_{e},

𝔪K,u=Hi​j​detH​ui​uj​d​S.\mathfrak{m}_{K,u}=H^{ij}\det{H}u_{i}u_{j}dS.

Given this, we can directly extend the definition of λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) for K∈𝒦eK\in{\mathcal{K}}_{e}, see [38, Section 1.4] for comparison. It is rather straightforward to see that λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) is upper semicontinuous with respect to the Hausdorff topology. The following problem seems to be really challenging and intriguing.

Conjecture 5.

The first even eigenvalue λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}) is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff topology of convex bodies. In other words, if hkh_{k} converges to hh in L∞L^{\infty}, then λ1,e​(−LKk)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K_{k}}) converges to λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}).

2. The Minkowski problem and variational approach

The variational approach for the LpL_{p} Minkowski problem, −n−1<p-n-1<p was introduced in the seminal work of Chou and Wang [18]. We will focus on the setting p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1). Let ff be a positive even smooth function on SnS^{n}. We define the probability measure induced by ff as

d​𝔪f=f​𝑑S​(∫Snf​𝑑S)−1.d\mathfrak{m}_{f}=fdS\left(\int_{S^{n}}fdS\right)^{-1}.

For an origin symmetric convex body KK with support function hh, we write d​SK=d​Sh=det(∇2h+h​Id)​d​SxdS_{K}=dS_{h}=\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})dS_{x} to be the surface area measure. More generally, for p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], d​Sh,p=h1−p​det(∇2h+h​Id)​d​SxdS_{h,p}=h^{1-p}\det(\nabla^{2}h+h\text{Id})dS_{x}. We also write the corresponding probability measure as

d​𝔪K,p=d​Sh,p​(∫Snd​Sh,p)−1.d\mathfrak{m}_{K,p}=dS_{h,p}\left(\int_{S^{n}}dS_{h,p}\right)^{-1}.

We prove our main theorem in this section. First we prove the following.

Our result gives a characterization of the uniqueness of even LpL_{p} Minkowski problem for p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), in terms of infλ1,e\inf\lambda_{1,e}. The conjecture [29, Section 5] asserts that infλ1,e=n+1\inf\lambda_{1,e}=n+1 (p0=0p_{0}=0). There are many evidences for the conjecture to hold in general, see [29, 39, 6] for more discussions. Note that the conjecture holds for n=1n=1 [7] and all known non-uniqueness results require p<0p<0. The L∞L_{\infty} estimate in [16] provides another evidence for p0=0p_{0}=0, which only works for p≥0p\geq 0 and fails for p<0p<0 [28]. We include a modification of their L∞L_{\infty} estimate below.

Remark 4.1.

Using the complex notations and plurisubharmonic functions to define the measures is only technical and auxiliary. The algebraic structure behind the operator is the well-known mixed volume in convex geometry and it corresponds to, essentially, the wedge product of corresponding matrices. The choice of complex notations is to use wedge product of forms, which is more transparent than the wedge product of matrices.

Similarly, Ui​j​δi​j​d​SU^{ij}\delta_{ij}dS is also a well-defined Radon measure for a convex body K∈𝒦eK\in{\mathcal{K}}_{e}. We now recall two equivalent definitions of the first even eigenvalue of −LK-L_{K} for any K∈𝒦eK\in{\mathcal{K}}_{e} as follows, when the convex body is in 𝒦+,e2{\mathcal{K}}^{2}_{+,e}. The first is the eigenvalue of the operator −LK-L_{K},

λ1,e​(−LK)=infu∈Ce2​(Sn)∫SnHi​j​h2​ui​uj​det(H)​𝑑S∫Sn(u−u¯)2​h​det(H)​𝑑S.\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K})=\inf_{u\in C^{2}_{e}(S^{n})}\frac{\displaystyle\int_{S^{n}}H^{ij}h^{2}u_{i}u_{j}\det(H)dS}{\displaystyle\int_{S^{n}}{(u-\underline{u})^{2}}h\det(H)dS}. (4.3)

for u−u¯≠0u-\underline{u}\neq 0. The second is essentially taking z=h​uz=hu in the above, and define

λ1,e​(K)=infz∈Ce2​(Sn)∫SnHi​j​zi​zj​det(H)​𝑑S−∫SnHi​j​δi​j​z2​detH​𝑑S+n​∫Snz2​h−1​detH​𝑑S∫Snz2​h−1​det(H)​𝑑S−(∫Snh​detH​𝑑S)−1​(∫Snz​detH​𝑑S)2.\lambda_{1,e}(K)=\inf_{z\in C^{2}_{e}(S^{n})}\frac{\displaystyle\int_{S^{n}}H^{ij}z_{i}z_{j}\det(H)dS-\int_{S^{n}}H^{ij}\delta_{ij}z^{2}\det{H}dS+n\int_{S^{n}}z^{2}h^{-1}\det{H}dS}{\displaystyle\int_{S^{n}}z^{2}h^{-1}\det(H)dS-\left(\int_{S^{n}}h\det{H}dS\right)^{-1}\left(\int_{S^{n}}z\det{H}dS\right)^{2}}. (4.4)

By our results above, both definitions extend to nonsmooth even convex bodies. Next, we prove that the two formulations are equivalent. The following is straightforward.

Our definition λ1,e​(−LK)\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}), in particular the formulation (4.4), is essentially the same with λC\lambda^{C} introduced in [41, 38]. There are two other natural notions [29, 38] to extend the definition to nonsmooth convex bodies. Let KiK_{i} be any sequence of convex bodies in 𝒦+,e2{\mathcal{K}}^{2}_{+,e} converging to KK, then one can introduce

It seems to be a very nontrivial problem whether, for a nonsmooth convex body K∈𝒦eK\in{\mathcal{K}}_{e} and n≥2n\geq 2,

λ¯1,e​(−LK)=λ¯1,e​(−LK)=λ1,e​(−LK).\underline{\lambda}_{1,e}(-L_{K})=\overline{\lambda}_{1,e}(-L_{K})=\lambda_{1,e}(-L_{K}).
